limitations: Bounded negative: only stage s875 was swept, and not all of its keys or dialogue actors; s885 and the remaining keys are named as the next places to look.
One session; no isolated review.
claims.derivation: Reached the stage with the developer warp, spawned its blocks, drove every reachable interaction, and logged the play entry and the register throughout.

claims.statement: Every stage's cast list is now read by one shared reader instead of two special cases: the player's own records and then every other actor whose gate passes, so the block actors finally appear on the fourteen screens that carry them - one of them standing exactly where the decode said it would.
claims.coverage: The reader's two loops ported with their gate semantics, one extractor decoding all 281 stages' lists (3595 records), the two old derived files reproduced byte for byte, and the assets manifest extended for the block pack.
limitations: The block interaction itself is implemented and unit-tested but its headless verification had not run at the time of writing, and its commit was pending.
The plus or minus one tick latch accounting in the interaction machine is chosen to reproduce the captured 36/41 totals; the capture cannot resolve the last tick.
claims.derivation: Ported the cast reader's two loops, decoded every stage's list, and wired the player and the general consumers.

claims.statement: Three more overworld touches are settled: a door shows the arrow its own tile's group calls for, doors only open when you face them (with a proof that turning away hides the arrow and refuses entry), ambushes fire from any facing - which the original does too, so our behaviour was already right - and the Submarimon hums while you hold the throttle, looping until you let go or lose the form.
claims.coverage: Each with a headless check: the door roundtrip derives the arrow kind from the grid group, the approach test adds the negative leg, the ambush verifier records the entry facing, and the Submarimon verifier proves the loop starts, sustains past the sample length and stops.
limitations: The ladder's extra clips turn out not to belong to the climb at all (they are another actor action), so nothing was wired - a negative finding, not a port.
The sparkle arming and orb gate, the confirm-probe box swap (blocked on a variant reconciliation) and the materialize halo (needs overlay decode work) remain open.
claims.derivation: Read each rule, implemented or proved the existing behaviour, and verified headlessly.

claims.statement: Three stage commands arm the player's sparkle actor (programs 1, 2 and 3); the fourth is not an arm at all, and the party orb is drawn only while the screen id is below the prologue cut, for the player only - so the orb appearing and the prologue ending are one and the same event.
claims.coverage: Both rules read out of the notify handler and the orb constructor, implemented once in the engine (sparkle program fold, party orb gate) and proved headlessly: the orb on a later screen with and without a party, absent at the cut, and both arm programs drawing.
limitations: An earlier note called the fourth command an arm and assumed a party-size test for the orb; both are corrected here.
claims.derivation: Lead integration of the 2026-10-06 worker results.

claims.statement: The two sounds an earlier sweep called unreachable are played in ordinary play: one cue plays the demo theme on seven stages and another plays the bird cue on two, both through the stage event command that sets an animation and a sound.
claims.coverage: The stage event jump table and its handler read out of the original, cross-checked by running the disc extractor, and the earlier negative explained: it swept the wrong stage and looked for a direct call rather than the data-driven trigger. The engine test re-derives every jump-table slot from the disc.
limitations: The sound table lists two cues that sit in a block only reachable from a higher command value - those ids are the silent slot, and the table row should be corrected.
claims.derivation: Lead integration of the 2026-10-06 worker results.

claims.statement: The small plate above the battle message box is the item list's quantity tag: an X label, a celframe behind it, and the carried count - or a dash pair when nothing is held. The walker already draws the same thing, so the panel an earlier note called missing was never missing.
claims.coverage: The three draw routines read out of the original with their bank words, the shipped string table pinning the X and dash-pair words to the observed plate, and a test that pins the plate's data identity; the item list itself is the default surface in the walker.
limitations: The 2026-10-05 live claim's clause that the walker draws no equivalent is wrong and is corrected by this claim.
claims.derivation: Lead integration of the 2026-10-06 worker results.

claims.statement: The geometry helper family - one per rotation order, scale, colour and the matrix multiply and solve - is identified by its body patterns rather than by guess, and the interpreter runs the coprocessor's register moves and its two geometry commands instead of stubbing them out.
claims.coverage: Family named by body comparison across the label ranges, a representative read per shape, the interpreter extended and its unit tests green, with the screen verifier still passing.
limitations: The card duel's remaining rig-bound effects (both-sides mask selection, the prompt-family latch, the third meaning of one field) are still open.
claims.derivation: Lead integration of the 2026-10-06 worker results.

claims.statement: The end-of-cast balloon is bounded: its ticker writes the height cap on both geometry paths, which an earlier read mistook for a constant load.
claims.coverage: Both stores read out of the original across the two geometry paths.
limitations: The live confirmation could not be photographed: at the operator's spot the cast resolved into a battle and the fishing field was torn down before the balloon appeared - a band-0 cast would settle it.
claims.derivation: Lead integration of the 2026-10-06 worker results.

claims.statement: The pad halo's claimed records are laid down in the stage's own table order rather than by tag number, so a stage whose table lists its tags out of order gets its pieces parked the other way round - which our engine had swapped.
claims.coverage: The claim walk read out of two stages and the third's out-of-order table, confirmed against the disc, implemented as a table-order claim, and pinned by a test that fails on the old code; the headless screen verifier passes including the affected stage's pad check.
limitations: Whether the swap is visible in play depends on paint order when the pieces share a position; no rig capture was taken.
The decor, single and rise claims' park order were not re-derived instruction by instruction.
The ten-slot instance budget was not shown to be exhausted in play.
claims.derivation: Lead integration of the 2026-10-06 worker results.

claims.statement: The in-place halo actor is now mined for twenty-six stages rather than eighteen: the eight new ones build it with their own allocator and run it without registering, so the effect appears where it was missing even though the stage never registers a member.
claims.coverage: The shape reader finds the variant without hand-written anchors, every newly mined stage's table was re-derived from the disc and matched by counts and values, and the three original stages reproduce byte-identically; two suites green.
limitations: Five copies whose arm writes the stepped value into every matching record are refused by name, because the first-match machine cannot express them.
Four overlays turn out to be a different actor (the stage root's sweep), and two stages belong to the slot-ensemble system instead.
claims.derivation: Lead integration of the 2026-10-06 worker results.

claims.statement: A routine that clears the ambush latch exists and zeroes the bitfield bytes covering the ambush flag, but nothing in the corpus calls it statically, so what clears the latch when the player leaves an area is still open.
claims.coverage: The routine read out of the executable with its store widths; the absence of a caller established by a full search of the corpus.
limitations: Needs a watch on the bitfield byte across a stage change to tie it to area exit.
claims.derivation: Lead integration of the 2026-10-06 worker results.

claims.statement: Nine functions - in the shop, the card-deck screens, the name screen, the training screens, the status screen and three others - are the same fade-start helper as the card-arm screen's, so one read names all nine.
claims.coverage: Each of the nine matched exactly one family, word-identical at gap zero to the known member with equal anchor vectors, and was previously unnamed; no function in the corpus matched more than one family.
limitations: The matcher's remaining misses are role-defined families - routines that share a job rather than a shape - which no body comparison reaches, so the honest ceiling is about fifty-four percent.
claims.derivation: Fixed the family matcher's body bound and precision, then propagated the names it unlocked.

claims.statement: Five cues that the sound table listed as playable play nothing: their compare branches sit in a block only reachable from command values the game never uses, so those ids are the silent slot.
claims.coverage: The disc's emote jump table read out and cross-checked by the extractor, which prints the silent slot for all five; the table's silent set now equals the binary's exactly, matching the engine module.
limitations: Nothing is lost by this: an earlier sweep already found which cues the game does play, and the demo theme and the bird cue are real, played by command from seven stages and two.
claims.derivation: Ran the emote extractor against the table and corrected the five rows.

claims.statement: A packed sound word that starts music is distinguishable by its bits: two high bits set with the top bit clear means a sequence rather than a sample, which is why an event can start a track where the sound-effects path would find nothing.
claims.coverage: Read out of the packed word's own encoding, implemented as the route in the walker, and pinned by a test that fails on the old routing; the stage event that starts the demo theme plays through the one music player because of it.
limitations: Only the single music-start word a field event uses is mapped to a track by name; a general word-to-stem table is not built, and the test that would settle it is to drive the game-over, evolution and stage tracks through the same route.
claims.derivation: Implemented the route the worker found and named the rule behind it.

claims.statement: A bulk pass named 179 previously unnamed routines across the executable, the battle stage, the field stage and the shop, card, training, naming and status screens - most off a single read per family, with the rest proven by exact match or recorded as siblings that differ only in which field they touch.
claims.coverage: Each name came from either a body-identical match verified at gap zero with equal anchors and a unique target, or a representative read carried to the family's members; the residue is listed by address per overlay rather than hidden.
limitations: The matcher cannot reach role-defined families, so roughly 500 routines remain as singletons needing one read each - listed per overlay in the residue files.
Two concurrent naming passes collided in the shared worktree, so some names landed inside another worker's commit; the counts were measured against the named baseline and are reported as such.
claims.derivation: Three workers ran the fixed matcher and the read-and-propagate protocol over the largest unnamed piles.

claims.statement: After a hit lands, a dispatcher looks up the technique's effect byte and runs the arm that applies its lasting consequence - poison, frozen, confusion, sleep, knock-out, drain or one of three stat penalties - writing the penalty to three halfwords on the fighter's roster record.
claims.coverage: The dispatcher, its thirty-three entry table, the penalty roll and the three appliers read out of the battle stage and ported into our own damage-terms module with a nine-case test; the whole suite is green.
limitations: Which roster member and which of the three halfwords carries which stat is not yet claimed - the per-stat mapping is unread, so the penalty producer is not wired and no guess was made.
The penalty dispatch ids are 32/33/34; an earlier equipment document states 26/27/28 and is corrected by this claim.
claims.derivation: Read the battle stage's unnamed functions as families, found the one genuinely missing behaviour and ported it.

claims.statement: The routines that looked like empty stubs are calls into the console's own library - file and card input-output, interrupt registration and pad start-up - and nine one-field setters are global flags whose bits one routine reads back as a weighted sum.
claims.coverage: Each thunk read per member from its own assembly with its library symbol, the two masked families identified as the same macro at two mask levels, and the flag setters read together with the routine that consumes them.
limitations: The names are assembly-read candidates, not runtime-verified.

One address in the executable resisted naming: it is the interior delayed-store half of a neighbour, still marked in the SDK disposition list by a masked sub-range match, and settling it would need the original linked symbol map.
claims.derivation: Read every flagged plumbing group once and carried the name to its members.

claims.statement: Whether a screen's ordinary route runs our code or the original's is now a measurement rather than an opinion: each screen is bundled and its reachable original-code set inspected, so the answer is 'ours', 'interpreter-reachable' or 'switch-gated only', with the line that decides it.
claims.coverage: Thirty screens and twelve systems measured; fourteen have no interpreter adapter at all; the harness is a test, so a new ordinary-route dependency on the original code fails the suite.
limitations: The measurement is static: it proves which modules are reachable, not that a screen behaves correctly.
The native reference routes remain by design behind explicit research switches and are not counted as production dependencies.
claims.derivation: Generalised the shop's execution-forbidden proof into a repo-wide harness.

claims.statement: The field's stage events are not the part still running through the original overlay: sixty-seven of the sixty-nine that carry no bytecode are handled by our own code - including the six Bug-Maze switch tiles - and the interpreter the ordinary field route still reaches is the stage-ambience overlay, which boots a stage's ambience actors natively.
claims.coverage: Every family of the sixty-nine named with a destination in our code, the census machine-checked as a test, the six switch events ported from their own stage's command handler and pad machine, and the ambiguity resolved by reading the field route's actual dependency.
limitations: Two events on one stage stay blocked: that stage ships two layouts and which cell reaches the second is undecoded, so nothing faithful could run.
The trap-tile mask is still one static layout; the switch writes the maze latch but does not draw a second mask.
claims.derivation: Took the natively-executed events as families and followed the route's real dependency.

claims.statement: The three halfwords a post-hit penalty writes are strength, defence and speed in that order, on the player's active party member, and two independent routines name the same three pairs.
claims.coverage: Read from the appliers' stride and from both readers - the shared effective-stat builder and the status sheet - with the older documents' apparent offset contradiction resolved as one halfword reached from two bases; wired into our damage terms with a test that derives the order from the reader rather than from a constant.
limitations: The engine's persistent member model still does not store the penalty halfwords, so nothing threads a live penalty into the player's record at runtime yet - the chain is producer to mapping to a pure consumer, tested end to end.
claims.derivation: Read the mapping from the disc's own two readers and wired it.

claims.statement: The Card Album, the folder editor and the card duel are genuine unported screens - their ordinary routes still build the original overlay and no session composes their translated fragments - unlike the shop, the lab and the measured fourteen, which were already ours and merely needed the proof.
claims.coverage: Measured per routine: album 19 of 28 translated (9 unported), folder editor 11 of 53 (42 unported), card duel about 60 of 319; the album's last three bodies ported and oracle-checked; the translated controllers proven to reach zero interpreter modules; the three routes pinned as interpreter-reachable in the frozen audit so the worklist cannot be silently reclassified.
limitations: What remains is composition, not translation: the album needs a session over its controllers plus two asset packs, the folder editor a session plus four picker callees, and the card duel a composed board, view presentation and match driver.
No browser capture was taken for these screens, and the ordinary routes were deliberately left unchanged rather than half-converted.
claims.derivation: Measured each screen's translated coverage against its overlay's routine count.

claims.statement: A stage's ambience actors - the objects a map boots when the player walks in - run our translated code on the ordinary field route, and the original overlay is reachable only behind a research flag.
claims.coverage: The decision line is gated so the interpreter is never called or fetched without the flag; the translated adapter declares its execution mode; the twelve translated ambience modules are measured by the audit harness; and a browser run with every native asset request aborted shows the ordinary route riding a stage actor and landing on its row while the reference flag boots the overlay.
limitations: The field is switch-gated-only rather than ours: web/native-stage.js is still statically linked into the shipped page, so the overlay code is present and one flag away - removing it is the bundle split.
One stage-object registry member (a screen-geometry object, not a display actor of this system) remains interpreter-only.
The quest-events, world-exploration and story-gating system rows still inherit the field's old decision line as a placeholder and need a real per-system measurement.
claims.derivation: Ported the ambience actors and moved the field's row from interpreter-reachable to switch-gated-only.

claims.statement: The console's own library routines can be named by importing community signature sets and symbol lists rather than by reading each body, and the imported pass is safe because it runs only where the repository's existing hash pass is silent and only inside the library zone.
claims.coverage: One hundred and twenty-eight routines named across nine libraries, with the unidentified residue falling from 333 to 144; a test proves a known body matches after import, that a wildcard byte may hold anything, that an unrelated body does not match, and that a placeholder names the library object rather than the routine.
limitations: Every name is a candidate identification by byte match, not verified behaviour, and none went through the review gate.

One hundred and forty-four addresses remain, in three blocks whose missing source is named: a LIBSD signature set for the sound bodies, a libspu symbol map with locals for the statics, and a memory-card symbol map for the interrupt internals.
Several of the public signature sets carry no licence file, so the fetched tree is kept untracked and only names and byte patterns are read.
claims.derivation: Imported public PSY-Q signature sets and symbol lists as a second matching pass.

claims.statement: Every field stage event that carries no bytecode of its own now runs our code: the last two were the Undersea Base room's inverse phase switches, decoded as a pair of layouts over one shared step-program table and ported.
claims.coverage: The census reads sixty-nine translated and zero blocked, with the layout pairing machine-checked as a test; the two events swap the active grid and program the trigger machine reads, through the room's phase latch.
limitations: The room's initial version at entry is chosen by a global written outside the stage (fieldstg's map-change branch), which was not folded in, so a re-entered room keeps its last phase.
Within one visit the disc's latch throws the switch at most once, so the pair alternates across visits rather than twice in one; the visible pacing was not confirmed in a browser.
Eight tests were failing in the shared tree during this work, all caused by another worker's in-flight edit to the same page file, none by these changes.
claims.derivation: Decoded the room's two layouts and ported the two events that swap them.

claims.statement: No page the game ships as production carries the console interpreter: the interpreter sits in a separate native bundle behind a single dynamic import, so a production route can neither execute it nor hide it as a fallback.
claims.coverage: The production barrel no longer exports the native modules; the page's built artefact and its static import graph both test clean for interpreter code; the research routes still load the native bundle deliberately; and the measured table's shipped-but-gated class disappeared entirely, leaving the three card screens and six placeholder system rows as the only interpreter reaches.
limitations: The native adapter modules are still statically imported by the page's scripts, but they contain no interpreter code and reach it only through the dynamic door - inert when their flags are off.

Six system rows and the three card screens still read interpreter-reachable; three workers are converting the card screens and the system rows need a real per-system measurement instead of their inherited placeholder line.
Two tests failed on the shared working tree during this work, both from sibling workers' in-flight card-screen conversions rather than from this change.
claims.derivation: Split the interpreter out of the production barrel into a flag-loaded native bundle and measured the effect.

claims.statement: The battle system is not fully translated: a hundred and ten decoded routines are unimplemented in our engine, dominated by the 3-D battle view's geometry, animation and effect pipeline - sixty-seven routines that run today through our own browser renderer rather than as a port of the original's.
claims.coverage: Measured one routine at a time against our implementation: fifty-seven decoded routines moved into the registry with real oracles, while the remaining hundred and ten are listed by group with what porting each would take rather than registered without a check.
limitations: The 3-D geometry, animation, effect-sprite and action-VM groups would each need their data flow decoded and a shared mesh/effect pipeline ported into the engine - the browser renderer is our own, not a port.
The action sequencer group (the twenty-four entry wfightmn arms and their status stagers) needs its own dispatcher ported.
Twenty-two loss, actor, HUD and equipment helpers are partially implemented but could not be pinned to a distinct port plus oracle, and were flagged rather than registered.
claims.derivation: Measured which decoded battle routines our engine genuinely implements.

claims.statement: The card folder editor is the first of the three card surfaces converted: its ordinary route runs our composed session and reaches no interpreter, with the original and the hand-made editor kept behind flags.
claims.coverage: A session over the existing controllers and shared shop services, three newly ported picker routines with an oracle comparing against the originals' own run, a browser verifier showing no executable asset request, and the untranslated parts registered as throwing stubs.
limitations: The editor's card grid and rename keyboard are not translated and their banks are not materialised, so the session stops there with a named error.
No registry rows were added for the new ports, and only the chooser journey was driven in the browser rather than every folder action.
A sibling worker overwrote two shared files mid-task, dropping this work; it was re-applied and both the album and folder routes were kept.
claims.derivation: Composed the folder editor's session and put the ordinary route on it.

claims.statement: The Card Album, the second of the three card surfaces converted, runs our composed session on the ordinary route with the original behind a flag, and its page mask runs on the screen object as the overlay's own call sites show.
claims.coverage: A session over the already-oracled album controllers and the shared shop services; the measured row turned to ours; a browser run through open, page turn, cursor and back with every native asset request aborted; and the album's chrome and text data extracted per language.
limitations: The card records' VRAM upload is called in order but takes no effect: our renderer paints from the extracted sheet and card atlas - a platform boundary, named in the session header.
A sibling's in-flight conversion left one flow-ownership test failing, which is not this screen's change, and the shared git index swept sibling files into this commit.
claims.derivation: Composed the album's session and put the ordinary route on it.

claims.statement: A fighter's 3-D presentation - which model, which texture patches, where it stands and which canned camera shot - is data on the disc, and that table with its variant selectors is ported and matches the originals' own execution.
claims.coverage: The presentation table's lookup, pool relocation, placement, camera shots and copy descriptor are ported and oracled against the originals' run; the two fidelity findings (an unsigned hover read, a full-word destination origin against a halfword source origin) came out of that comparison.
limitations: The 3-D core - vertex projection, the layer builder's matrix passes and the display-list packing - is decoded in prose but not ported: an oracle first needs the console's coprocessor moves modelled in our interpreter.
The effect-sprite system is decoded but not ported, and the per-tick variant loop was not run end to end.
The browser's battle renderer still carries its own hand-written copies of what is now ported, which the shared-system rule says to replace.
claims.derivation: Ported the presentation table and oracled it against the originals' run.

claims.statement: The card duel's remaining work is a layer, not the seventeen-item list: below the mode updates sits a further group of duel routines that no engine module implements, so the pieces must be ported by mechanism rather than one at a time.
claims.coverage: Five of the named pieces are ported with an oracle against the originals; the mode updates were read far enough to name the layer beneath them and the four view-method slots one of the ported pieces dispatches through.
limitations: The ordinary route deliberately stays on the overlay: a session that stalls after its banner would present a partial flip as done.
The newly named layer's routines are named, not yet read.
claims.derivation: Followed the named gaps and found the layer beneath them.

claims.statement: Measured per surface, only two routes still reach the interpreter: the card duel screen, which is still being ported, and the interpreter itself - so every other player-facing system's ordinary route runs our code.
claims.coverage: Forty of forty-two top-level surfaces are ours with the shipped-but-gated class gone, and the six system rows that had inherited a placeholder verdict are replaced by per-surface measurements, with the two mixed systems recorded as their components rather than rounded.
limitations: The card duel and the interpreter are the two honest reaches; the interpreter row is correct as long as the research routes exist.
Whether a route calls the native loader or merely imports it is not statically distinguishable, so the measurement is the module graph reaching the native bundle.
The derived per-system manifests were left stale rather than regenerated with unrelated drift.
claims.derivation: Measured each system's own routes instead of inheriting the field's placeholder line.

claims.statement: The fighter's 3-D look in the browser is driven by the ported disc system rather than a hand-written copy: placement, the eye/blink/body patch choice and the patch copy rectangle all come from the port, and the visible output is unchanged.
claims.coverage: The browser's selectors and placement consume the ported module through a standing guard test; the before-and-after captures of 1665 variant and rectangle events and 498 placements are byte-identical, and the real WebGL verifier reports zero bytes wrong.
limitations: The renderer's other modules are its own implementations of routines with no engine port yet (the camera, action VM, actor animator, timeline, effect player and projection layers), so they remain per-case code until those routines are ported.
The committed page bundle was built from the live tree and carries siblings' uncommitted engine source; it must be rebuilt once those land.
claims.derivation: Rewired the browser renderer onto the ported presentation module and captured before and after.

claims.statement: The card folder editor runs entirely on our code with no part of it refusing: its card grid and rename keyboard are ported, the keyboard by reusing the shared name-entry implementation it is a byte-for-byte copy of, and its four text banks are materialised.
claims.coverage: The card grid ported from the overlay's bodies with an oracle over nine hundred seeded machine states, the keyboard re-driving the shared name-entry module, the composed journey running both hand-offs with no throw, and the execution-forbidden check extended to the new modules.
limitations: The shared card-view text context is left as a host boundary, as the album also treats it: the detail panel shows the card's colour from our compact table rather than its real attack, health and cost values, and the card-art primitive is replaced by the extracted atlas.
No browser check was run for this screen; the verification is the composed-session test and data-path checks.
This work landed inside a sibling's commit because the tree shares one git index, with a second record commit carrying its own message.
claims.derivation: Ported the folder editor's remaining grid and keyboard and materialised its banks.

claims.statement: The console coprocessor the battle 3-D core depends on is modelled in our interpreter, so the vertex projection and the layer builder's parent-chain passes are ported and match the original instruction words - and one decode defect in our own interpreter, which made the projection's store trap, is fixed.
claims.coverage: Registers and every command the overlay contains are modelled with evidence from the disc's own sites and the documented encoding; the projection and the composite-layer passes are oracled against the original words run through our interpreter, with hand-computed command tests and negative controls.
limitations: The coprocessor arithmetic follows the published documentation and hand-computed cases, not a console trace; a fight-time capture of the coprocessor registers would settle it.
The display-list interpreter and its packers, the layer builder's surrounding steps and the effect-mesh colour path are not ported.
The projection is not yet registered as a translated function, and the ported core is not yet wired into the browser renderer.
claims.derivation: Modelled the coprocessor and oracled the projection and layer composite against the original words.

claims.statement: The browser renderer's implementations of battle routines are not ports and are not registered as such, even where they behave correctly: the registry holds no browser module, so the routines that live only there - the camera and face-box loops, a cel draw, an enemy-id resolver, a slow-motion stepper, a result-queue walk and the steal roll - count as unimplemented until ported from the disc.
claims.coverage: Each flagged routine was traced to what our code does with the same state: four are backed by an exported engine function and gained registry rows with real oracles, and the other eighteen are named by group with what a port would take.
limitations: Some of the eighteen are browser-implemented and behave correctly today; the distinction is evidence, not visible behaviour.

A few are partial: the poison and sleep appliers exist only as dispatcher-table entries, the result queue's geometry is ported but its walk is not, and only the steal routine's accessory-byte fold is ported.
claims.derivation: Traced each flagged routine to our implementation rather than to a name.

claims.statement: A single walk of the game with no research flag reaches every major surface and runs our code: the opening, a battle with its command list, the field, a talk, the pause, a shop purchase, the album, the folder editor and the digivolution lab, with no executable asset requested and no uncaught error.
claims.coverage: A harness that boots the real page, aborts every native asset request, asserts each screen's translated execution mode and screenshots each step; the research routes were separately verified to still boot the original deliberately.
limitations: The shop, album, folder and lab were reached through the page's lab entry points because their in-game triggers need story progress the opening does not provide; the screens themselves are the shipped modules.
The card duel was not walked (its match is still being ported), and the walk stops after the second map.
One finding is unresolved gameplay rather than tooling: our opening hands off with a random encounter already running, which is queued to be settled against the disc.
claims.derivation: Walked the ordinary route end to end in one browser session.

claims.statement: A card's detail panel shows the card's real record - its attack, health, kind, level and cost - because the resident card-view text context is ported once and both the album and the folder editor read it, replacing the colour-only table they each carried.
claims.coverage: The records are materialised at the selector's own stride, the selector's file and record arithmetic follows the canonical card document, the newly ported sprite primitive is oracled byte-for-byte with its ordered emit calls, and both screens' before-and-after captures show real values.
limitations: A Program card's summon cost is absent from the extracted catalogue, so that field is written as zero until the extractor carries it.
The folder editor's own stat line did not render in the captured states, so its evidence is the capture JSON and the composition test rather than that screenshot.
claims.derivation: Ported the shared card-view context and wired both card screens to it.

claims.statement: In our disassembly, the subtract instruction is printed in two-operand form, so its first operand is also the destination and is included in the result - a reader who takes it as three-operand form gets a sign error, which is exactly what happened to the 3-D matrix builder's first reading.
claims.coverage: Found by an oracle that compares the ported matrix against the original instruction words on ten fixed and five hundred random angle triples, with a negative control.
limitations: The trap applies to any routine read from the same disassembly; the affected readings have not yet been swept.
claims.derivation: The matrix oracle's failure exposed the two-operand form.

claims.statement: A DNA confirm reaches the battle's action layer through the controller's own step and a direct call into the field overlay, not through the action table - so it has no arm and no queue kind, and a document that named one is wrong.
claims.coverage: The command phase's action code, the controller's step entry and the call target are machine-checked in the module and its tests; the refuted address holds a data word in the field overlay whose value resembles another overlay's code, and the offset it was said to swap is the generic task-state method.
limitations: A canonical battle document still carries the refuted line and needs the correction, along with any other note derived from it.
claims.derivation: Followed the DNA step from the controller to its callee and checked the words.

claims.statement: An attacker's travel to its target during a basic attack is a ported disc system that the browser consumes, with the same trajectories as before the rewire - and the browser's release of the attack wait is one tick earlier than the original's state machine, a divergence that is documented rather than corrected.
claims.coverage: The controller, its factory and its motion curves are oracled against the original instruction words every tick, with negative controls; the six models' before-and-after trajectories are byte-identical.
limitations: The divergence in when the wait releases is kept deliberately, so the strike frame may differ from the original by one tick; it is not yet settled whether that is visible.

The action VM's dispatcher and its eight opcode handlers are still implemented in the browser, as are the timeline sampler, effect player, actor animator, idle director, camera, projection layers and coordinator.
claims.derivation: Ported the slot-motion controller and rewired the browser onto it.

claims.statement: The battle waiting on arrival at the second map is the disc's own scripted stage-entry encounter, fired by an event the stage's entry dispatcher starts when the story ordinal and a flag agree - not a random encounter, and not a divergence in our handoff.
claims.coverage: The entry dispatcher's gate and the event's completion chain are read from the stage's own overlay with the gate table's rows; a live probe of the ordinary opening shows the fight begins through the screen entry, never the random path, with the encounter counter unchanged and every route stage at rate zero; three tests pin the chain.
limitations: Only this stage's arrival script and the seven stages on the opening route were checked; other stages' arrival battles were not re-derived.
The earlier explanation recorded in the playthrough document (an expired encounter counter) was wrong and has been corrected there.
claims.derivation: Settled the arrival fight from the stage's own script plus a live probe of the ordinary route.

claims.statement: Our listings print a subtract in shortened form when its source equals its destination, so the first operand is also the result - a reading trap that applies to four fifths of the subtract lines and is now documented where a reader meets it.
claims.coverage: The rule was proved by decoding the raw instruction words across the entire corpus and reproducing every printed line; an oracle pins it and four sub-derived strides against the original words; and every port deriving a value from a subtract was checked, with one wrong case found - already corrected.
limitations: The formatter is outside this repository, so the rule is documented rather than fixed at source.
The corpus check leaves a handful of mismatches explained by a register-naming alias, not by a second rule.
claims.derivation: Swept every subtract-derived port and proved the printing rule from the raw words.

claims.statement: The card catalogue carries every field a card record holds - costs, level, rank and combo - so a missing value in our data now means the disc holds zero rather than that nobody read it.
claims.coverage: Each field's offset and width was verified against the raw records for all 316 cards and pinned by a test that recomputes them independently; both card screens read the catalogue's own fields, and the folder editor's stat line is captured with its widgets visible.
limitations: One byte is zero on every card and has no established meaning, so it is deliberately not emitted.
A Program card's summon cost is genuinely zero on the disc, so it stays zero honestly rather than being filled in.
claims.derivation: Verified every record field against the raw card data and carried them all.

claims.statement: An effect in battle is a flat sprite driven by rows that overwrite only the channels their mask selects - clip, colour shift, offset, scale and three angles - and our engine now steps and draws it from the disc, with the sprite projecting through the camera only in world space.
claims.coverage: The stepper and draw are ported and oracled against the original instruction words after every call, comparing all nine channels, the cursor, call counts and a gate, with negative controls; the browser's effect player consumes the port and a 3048-tick capture is byte-identical.
limitations: A row step above one now skips rows as the original does, where our old loop caught up - slow motion is the only case that changed.
The effect object family driver, the display-list loop (undecoded, rig capture queued) and several action-VM handlers are not ported.
claims.derivation: Ported the channel-record stepper and the draw, and rewired the browser onto them.

claims.statement: Where two battle routines differ only in their constants, one port covers both: the task spawner and the readout constructor share the same mechanism with different arguments, so the second is a data variant rather than a second implementation.
claims.coverage: Both were read, the shared mechanism was ported once, and the variant is named in the registry and the report; the other six routines of the group each got their own port and oracle.
limitations: The shared barrel file these ports are exported from references modules that are not yet committed by sibling workers, so the tree is not independently buildable until they land.
claims.derivation: Grouped the remaining routines by mechanism and ported one representative per family.

claims.statement: The face box in a 3-D battle always frames the player's own partner, regardless of which side is speaking - the speaker selects between two framings stored on that fighter - and it draws nothing when the framing's projection distance is not positive.
claims.coverage: The four-routine family and the resident look-at helper family are ported and oracled against the original instruction words with a negative control per case; the browser consumes the port and the capture shows every consumed field unchanged.
limitations: The console services the box's worker needs are injected as a host boundary, since they belong to the effect, timeline and HUD systems other workers own.

The integer square root the look-at uses drives two coprocessor registers the interpreter does not model, so that routine is pinned against the disc's table and a floor-square-root reference rather than against the running original.
claims.derivation: Ported the camera look-at and the face-box family and rewired the browser.

claims.statement: The per-tick controller that owns a spawned effect set is the driver behind the transformation screen's fifteen-step presentation; its step dispatch is ported and oracled, and its fifteen step bodies are a separate job.
claims.coverage: The entry and construct-stage dispatch, the fifteen-entry jump table and its timer gates are ported, with an oracle that records which entry the original jumps to for each candidate; the projectile lookup and constructor are ported with the flight's travel reused from another worker's port.
limitations: The fifteen step bodies and the four construct-stage bodies are not ported: each drives three sub-managers through roughly twenty external entry points, and the screen's observable output today comes from the blast-presentation module rather than from them.
The effect-sound and slot-overlay routines the action VM's op10 and op7 call were not attempted.
claims.derivation: Ported the projectile lookup/constructor and the effect-family driver's dispatch.

claims.statement: Between actions the battle shows one of four fixed framings chosen by the idle director, with a slow orbit while it holds, and a scripted move names one of a fighter's four animation slots whose table, home point and travel deltas our engine now computes from the disc.
claims.coverage: Both systems are ported and oracled against the original instruction words - three thousand ticks for the director, six cases for the slot resolver, table bind, placement and the movement arms - with the browser rewired and the actor trajectory byte-identical.
limitations: Two ports of the same slot-finder now exist (this one and another worker's pool module), and they must be reconciled to one under the shared-system rule.
One module under the systems tree is not yet claimed by the catalog, and the remaining movement modes and the director's third state are not ported.
claims.derivation: Ported the idle camera director and the animation-slot system with oracles.

claims.statement: When a card is played in the duel, the slots it may hit are lit by that card's filter class - nine behaviours ranging from 'mark nothing', through 'test side and colour', to 'mark everything the board does not hold' - and the HUD's numbers are repainted from the row sums with each colour clamped.
claims.coverage: Both the commit boundary and the counter service are ported and oracled against the originals across all ten filter classes and the full repaint, with the tests shown to fail when an arm is mutated; the modules are added to the duel's execution-forbidden controller list.
limitations: The opponent AI and the nine mode updates remain, so the ordinary route is still not flipped and a duel cannot be played to its end.
The pre-commit hook's regeneration staged three generated files carrying a concurrent worker's inputs; they were not hand-staged.
claims.derivation: Ported the duel's commit boundary and counter service with discriminating oracles.

claims.statement: Which actor reacts to a landed attack, on which side and with which clip, is the original's own subordinate-dispatch handler rather than a rule for the browser to decide inline, and it is now a port fed by the browser's data.
claims.coverage: The handler's mode logic (which destroys and replaces a child actor, inverting its side, and writes its clip) and the companion reaction machine's fourteen-word table are ported and oracled against the original words over a grid of modes, sides and outcomes, with negative controls and an unchanged thirty-three-scenario capture.
limitations: The reaction machine's individual case bodies - the clips, parameters and damage for each hit kind - are not ported, nor is the attack data that authors which reaction kind is used; the worker named the region that would settle it rather than guessing.
The mesh-animator constructor wrapper for the 3-D chain remains unported.
claims.derivation: Ported the subordinate-dispatch handler and the reaction-kind table.

claims.statement: The original writes an attacker's pose before advancing its travel timer, so our browser had been releasing the attack's wait one call late; the fix makes the new trajectory equal the port exactly, with the strike ticks and travel distances unchanged.
claims.coverage: The divergence was measured (release at ramp call 62 against our 63, poses identical, landing the same tick), fixed in the browser's step, and proven with a capture where the trajectory matches the port and the strike ticks stay 25/20/20/20.
limitations: The dispatch decoder still frames one opcode as five words where the handler consumes six; the mis-frame is masked in shipped data but is a real tool defect.
Several handler bodies remain unported (the effect, camera, anim-manager and actor-factory targets), now that those subsystems exist they are the next step.
claims.derivation: Settled the timing divergence from the disc and ported the sampler and dispatcher.

claims.statement: The free-roam camera follows the player exactly, with no lag and no dead zone: it copies the leader's position every frame, centres it at 160 by 140 in map pixels and lets only the map edge stop it.
claims.coverage: The controller and its submitter are read from the field overlay with their immediates, the rule is implemented once as a shared camera module and consumed by the ordinary camera path, and a live verifier shows the camera landing where the disc's arithmetic expects while four other checks stay green.
limitations: The camera shake is not ported: its table lies past the end of the field listing and its trigger is unlocated.
The centre rests on the disc's immediates and a live arithmetic check rather than a frame capture of the original.
claims.derivation: Decoded the camera follow rule from the overlay and implemented it as one shared system.

claims.statement: A generated bundle committed to the tree must be a build of the committed source, not of whatever was in the working tree at the time - and until it is, every suite failure it causes looks like a defect.
claims.coverage: The committed page bundle was found carrying an export that existed only in uncommitted work; a rebuild from a pristine archive of the committed tree was committed, and the bundle's hash now equals a clean rebuild's exactly, with the barrel verified to export every module it names.
limitations: While workers are live the bundle can be re-polluted by any rebuild they run; the hygiene check has to be repeated at the end of a parallel session.
claims.derivation: Reconciled the duplicate port and re-verified the generated artefacts against the committed tree.

claims.statement: The card duel's opponent chooses without randomness and keeps the lowest board score among the slots it can hit - so it aims at the strongest target available rather than conserving cards - and its legality gate is the same test the player's cursor uses.
claims.coverage: The think pause, the legality gate with its two collection probes, the board scoring with its combo grouping, the target choice and the narrowing helpers are ported and oracled against the originals over every arm, mask, side and run length, with a mutation test that fails on three separate altered constants.
limitations: The routine that actually picks the card from the hand and the Program simulator are not ported, so a match still cannot be played to its end and the ordinary route stays on the overlay.
No whole-match proof was run - it is impossible without the pick.
claims.derivation: Ported the duel AI's decision layer with discriminating oracles.

claims.statement: A night of changes to the battle systems, the card screens, the field camera and the shipped bundle left the ordinary route intact: a fresh end-to-end walk passes every step and shows the new systems rendering.
claims.coverage: The same harness re-run at a HEAD forty-six commits past its baseline, with a new camera check, card-detail checks and battle-rewire checks added, and every difference from the baseline classified - the camera and the ported systems as expected improvements, a per-frame counter and press timing as benign, and one harness race diagnosed rather than filed as a defect.
limitations: The walk exercises the on-disk bundle rather than a pinned commit, since workers were editing the tree during the run.
The album and folder detail popups were not opened on screen because the ordinary route starts with an empty collection.
Coverage is still the opening: nothing past the second map is walked because the story does not progress that far.
claims.derivation: Re-ran the ordinary-route walk after a night of commits and classified every difference.

claims.statement: The transformation a player watches is a fifteen-step choreography of spawned effects and camera moves, and its bodies are ported with their call trace and store sequence checked against the originals - though our presentation already produces the visible result and both agree on every effect spawned.
claims.coverage: All fifteen step bodies and the four construct-stage bodies are ported and oracled across every substate, stage and two branch scenarios, with the fallthrough composition that is real code; the oracle caught six reading errors, and the two independent derivations of the effect sets agree.
limitations: The sub-manager services the bodies call remain host stubs, which is the last dependency before the screen itself can be declared execution-forbidden.
The ported bodies are not wired into the visible path by design, since doing so would replace a working presentation.
claims.derivation: Ported the transformation driver's step bodies and oracled them against the original words.

claims.statement: Our action-script decoder framed one opcode shorter than the handler consumes, and the skipped word - a zero - was read as an end-of-script marker, cutting twenty-two Digimon's scripts short at their first such record; the framing is fixed and those scripts are restored.
claims.coverage: The handler's own pointer arithmetic sets the advance to six words; re-extracting showed twenty-two models changed, one script each; the census baseline, the technique-result grouping and the clip segmentation were all updated to match, and every suite is green.
limitations: Two opcodes still use the browser's own blocking and yield protocol, since that lives in the virtual machine's cursor rather than the handlers.
A lead-owned research document still describes the old framing and its supposed barriers.
claims.derivation: Ported the opcode handlers onto the existing subsystem ports and fixed the decoder's framing.

claims.statement: The reaction kind a hit produces is authored at runtime by the battle command executor from the actor's status and conditions, not by a per-technique table - so no static mapping from attack to reaction kind exists, and the two fields' link has no store anywhere in the code.
claims.coverage: The machine's input field is read from the original; the typed kinds' author is identified with the assignments it makes; the region a previous worker named as the source is shown, over the committed disc image, to be an action record of an unrelated table whose column never holds a typed kind; and the case bodies themselves are ported and oracled with a discriminating mutation.
limitations: The runtime watch that would tie a specific attack to a kind has not been run - it needs the emulator and a RAM watch on the actor's fields.

The executor that authors the kinds is not itself ported, and one address is now registered twice in the translated-function registry (as the reaction machine and as item use), which needs reconciling.
claims.derivation: Ported the reaction case bodies and refuted the supposed static kind source.

claims.statement: The duel opponent's card choice declines to play when it is already ahead of the player's board but commits on a tie, answers a played card with the complementary counter class where the card calls for one, and marks only the first candidate passing its three gates.
claims.coverage: The pick, the worth-it test and the counter simulator are ported from the overlay assembly with oracles over every branch, both call orders and a tie case, and six mutants each make the oracle fail; the defect the earlier module carried at a tie is fixed.
limitations: A whole match still cannot be played: the nine mode updates and the effect-VM step are not ported, and each mode update calls a further layer no module implements, so porting them alone moves the gap down one level rather than closing it.
The pick is exposed on the session for a future match driver but no match driver exists yet.
claims.derivation: Ported the duel AI's card choice and named the remaining blocker by running a match and reporting the failure.

claims.statement: Sixteen specific story beats change the overworld's background music: on each, the scene's music track is re-stored to a different track of the same area archive, keyed off the master story ordinal.
claims.coverage: Both of the disc's own jump tables are read and their sixteen-entry sets agree; the rule is implemented once as a shared scene variant, wired into the walker's music call, with a test that re-derives the set from the tables and asserts the browser mirror matches.
limitations: The proof is the disc-grounded test rather than a browser capture, because the difference is audible rather than visible.
The display-slot flag the same beats set is decoded and exposed but not consumed: which resident slot it lands on depends on the table's tag walk, and that arm was not shown being reached in play.
claims.derivation: Decoded the sixteen-ordinal scene variant and replaced a mis-described gap row with the real mechanism.

claims.statement: Our transformation sequence reproduces the effects and their order from the disc, but its frame timings come from a recorded capture rather than from the disc's own frame mapping - so the state machine cannot be substituted in until that mapping is read, because the two would differ in timing.
claims.coverage: The spawner and the driver's host seam are ported and oracled, the presentation's effect set and order are confirmed to match the driver's, and the wiring was declined with the exact missing evidence named - the disc's frame mapping for the spawns.
limitations: The screen is not execution-forbidden: the service callbacks the driver's bodies invoke are still host services, though the real ports they route to are named and oracle'd in their own modules.
No end-to-end oracle covers the whole call graph; the spawner and the routing are proven separately.
claims.derivation: Ported the effect spawner and the driver host, and declined the wiring with the missing evidence named.

claims.statement: Both action opcodes whose blocking and waiting lived outside the handlers are now driven by the port: the blocking one rewinds its cursor while the motion object it waits on is armed, and the waiting one latches a frame count and advances on release.
claims.coverage: Both ports are read from the overlay assembly with their exact rewinds and advances, oracled against the original's continue flag and cursor behaviour, rewired into the browser, and captured byte-identical; the one behavioural difference they cause is bounded and documented.
limitations: Twenty-eight wait records across eleven models now yield one extra tick than the old browser's rule, which is a deliberate correction and not visible in the captured five models.
One further block, the mode-0 bound-table wait, is still supplied by the browser.
Two comment sites still describe the chunk boundaries as end-of-script barriers, and are queued for a one-line fix.
claims.derivation: Ported the action VM's remaining cursor protocol onto the handlers and corrected the records that described the old framing.

claims.statement: The card duel's remaining chain is entirely static and closable, not blocked: 246 routines are reachable from its entry points, 158 unported, and 56 of them are installed through constructors so they are absent from the lifted C - but nothing in it needs the emulator.
claims.coverage: Every entry point was followed through its jump tables and calls with counts, the two self-contained phases are ported and oracled with a mutation, and a whole-match verifier prints the per-step gap report; two full suites pass.
limitations: The ported chain is two phases of eleven, so a match still cannot complete and the ordinary route stays on the original.
The 56 constructor-installed routines need lifting before the arms that call them can be ported.
The spinner cannot be left by a tick-only driver, so any match driver must also drive the board's draw pass.
claims.derivation: Measured the duel's remaining porting chain to its leaves and ported its two self-contained phases.

claims.statement: The flag the field's sixteen variant beats set lands on the first record of the stage's ambient display chain whose tag byte is one, and it lights that record on those beats - so a small wall decoration appears only on the sixteen.
claims.coverage: The chain walk is read from the disc's raw words, implemented once as a shared rule and consumed by the effects path, checked live on three stages including one with no tagged record, and covered by tests that re-derive the first match from the words; a before/after capture shows the decoration on and off.
limitations: The compiler's lifted output drops the first record's tag, so any future reading of this walk must take the raw words.
Three neighbouring rows were already done (the gondola backdrop, the NPC default facing and a scene record count), and the wipes remain: they build raw display tags and need the emulator.
claims.derivation: Decoded the display-chain walk from the raw words, implemented it and consumed the flag.

claims.statement: The transformation's spawn timing is part statically fixed and part runtime-gated: two spawn moments are disc constants while the last waits on a spawned overlay's readiness, and the sequence's start waits on an asset being resident - so a recording's phase boundaries are not the same quantity as the driver's spawn frames.
claims.coverage: The driver is run word for word through the emulator-interface once per frame for the whole program, its spawn table is asserted with a negative control, and the two runtime gates are identified with the fields they poll; the runtime watch that would settle the remainder is named, with the addresses that must not be watched because they crash or throttle the rig.
limitations: The final spawn's frame and the sequence's start are not settled, so the state machine is deliberately not wired into the presentation.
The named watch has not been run.
claims.derivation: Decoded the transformation's spawn gates and measured where the recording and the disc differ.

claims.statement: The card duel's board installs fifty-six routines through constructors, and every one of them already has readable lifted C - the count that suggested otherwise was the disassembler's entry list, which a constructor-installed routine never joins.
claims.coverage: Installed, lifted and absent counts are checked directly against the tree; a fresh lift of the overlay reproduces all fifty-six files byte for byte; the routines are grouped into fourteen named families with one representative read each, and the one that needed a jump-table patch is committed with its patched listing.
limitations: The tool's own list command still reports fifty-one as missing because the overlay's entry list was not updated - a display bug, not a gap, and it is queued.
One routine (0x8009ce94) remains unnamed for want of a caller in the overlay.
The duel's real blocker is the mode machine's arms and the board's draw pass, not the listings.
claims.derivation: Checked the installed-routine premise against the tree and grouped the routines into families.

claims.statement: Across 49 measured surfaces the ordinary route runs our code on 41 and reaches the original interpreter in exactly two places: the card duel, which is mid-port, and the interpreter itself.
claims.coverage: The audit re-runs at the night's HEAD, every surface's class is checked against the recorded JSON, the negative control catches a linked interpreter both as a source module and as code inside a built bundle, and the production bundle and page graph are confirmed interpreter-free.
limitations: A surface measuring ours means no interpreter is reached, NOT that the mechanism is a ported one - the battle's 3-D layer measures ours while at least one of its mechanisms is still browser-authored, which is why a faithfulness measure is owed.
Catalog rows in five systems still carry the pre-split 'switch-gated-only' mark, and the screen-progress note still quotes the pre-split table.
claims.derivation: Re-ran the execution-forbidden audit after the night's ports and corrected its own definition of a surface.

claims.statement: The battle's 3-D layer draws from a display list whose byte's high nibble selects the handler - zero for a mesh emission dispatched on the low nibble, otherwise a seven-entry table setting a layer state value - and every opcode's cursor advance is now measured from a live stream, including a mesh emission's size-dependent step.
claims.coverage: Two model nodes' lists are dumped from a live battle and decoded against the loop's own words; per-opcode advances are measured; the loop's uncovered opcode ranges are identified and shown unused by any shipped stream; the mesh colour path's inputs and outputs are captured as the registers the routine programs.
limitations: The emulator cannot read the coprocessor register file, so the colour path's values are the general registers it programs - one step removed from a register snapshot.
Only two of eighteen model lists were dumped, and the identity of each group was not tied to a particular creature.
Nothing was ported in this pass.
claims.derivation: Captured the display-list stream and the colour path's registers from a live battle on the rig.

claims.statement: The fight's ordinary route consumes four of thirteen mechanisms as real ports while three are still browser-authored and six are mixed - and several modules ported in the same session are exported but imported by nothing, so their work is invisible to a player.
claims.coverage: Every mechanism is classified with file:line evidence on both sides, a checker encodes the table and fails on drift, and the unconsumed ports are listed individually - including one module that no browser file imports at all.
limitations: The audit's own definition of the fight surface derives 'no interpreter' from the ports rather than from the page's imports, so it cannot see an unconsumed port; the fix is proposed in the document but not applied.
No frame-level comparison of the ported handler bodies against a live battle has been run.
Wiring the unconsumed ports is not done and is the next campaign.
claims.derivation: Measured the fight's 3-D layer mechanism by mechanism against the ordinary route's imports.

claims.statement: The ordinary route past the opening works in our build: nine later areas are walkable with translated ambience, a wild battle in a later sector completes, and the gym runs its translated flow - while the arena finale and the arena floor remain unverified.
claims.coverage: A committed walker boots each area from a fixture, screenshots it, asserts the translated markers, starts a later-sector battle and completes it, enters the gym and runs its states, and reports every failure with its exact error; the same walker reproduced the session's crash on the broken tree.
limitations: No conversation starts the arena finale - it may be gated on a story flag - and the arena floor boots with no NPCs and no exits; both are unverified rather than known-broken.
One stage's fixture spawn pins the player at the map origin, which is not settled as a gap or a freeze.
This verifies our build, not the original: a browser walk is the weakest evidence class and cannot establish original behaviour.
claims.derivation: Walked the ordinary route past the opening and verified the later areas, a later-sector battle and the gym.

claims.statement: The execution-forbidden measurement now records, for every port it credits to a surface, whether the ordinary route actually imports it - so an exported but unused module can no longer read as covering a mechanism.
claims.coverage: Consumedness is derived from the page's static import graph through the engine's symbols to their defining modules, closed transitively, carried as a column and its own report section with the classes left untouched, and controlled by stripping an import to watch the port flip and by crediting nothing for an empty import set.
limitations: Seven of the fight's twenty-one ports are unconsumed and are the wiring campaign's list, not a defect in the measurement.
The committed JSON is a snapshot: the tree was being edited by several workers while it was generated.
Consumedness is module-level; whether a particular function inside a consumed module is called is the faithfulness checker's statement, not the audit's.
claims.derivation: Added a derived consumedness column to the audit so an unused port cannot be credited to a surface.

claims.statement: The transformation driver's camera-manager and animation-object callees are real ports now, and several other callees resolve to services that already existed rather than new code - but the animation manager's own method and the instance allocator remain host services, so the screen still cannot be called execution-forbidden.
claims.coverage: Both new port families are read from the overlay assembly with their constructor-installed offsets, oracled against the original words with mutations that fail, and the reused services are confirmed by reading the disc image at the offsets that invoke them; the host's previously wrong inline arm is corrected.
limitations: The animation manager's own +0xe8 method, the animation-instance allocator, the effect-object allocator and several service boundaries remain host-supplied, which is why the screen is not execution-forbidden.
No driver run over the real subsystem has been compared against a capture.
The ports are consumed by the transformation path only; the ordinary battle's consumption of the wider battle ports is a separate measurement.
claims.derivation: Ported the transformation driver's remaining callees onto real services and oracled them.

claims.statement: The battle's display-list dispatch loop is a port whose cursor trace matches the original's own words running over a live-captured byte stream, store for store, and it selects the same packet builder the original selects - but the shipped geometry does not yet carry the raw bytes, so the ordinary route is still fed by the extractor's hand-written decode.
claims.coverage: The loop, its per-class handling, its mesh advance and its descriptor word are read from the overlay assembly and oracled against the original loop's own words over two captured streams, with a mutation that breaks the comparison and a guard that the dump is the right routine; the browser route has a path that consumes the port when a layer carries raw bytes.
limitations: No shipped geometry carries the raw bytes yet, so the ported path is present but unfed and the visible picture is unchanged.
The mesh-emission path's own packet-field build and its projected-sign cull are not ported, which is why fifteen of eighteen instructions are culled by code we do not have.
The effect-mesh colour path is not ported, and its capture is a register-in/out form rather than a register snapshot.
claims.derivation: Ported the display-list loop and proved it against the live-captured byte stream.

claims.statement: The card duel's draw phase and its draw families are ports, and driving the draw pass takes a whole match out of mode one for the first time - but a match still does not complete, and the next block is the routine that runs a queued effect opcode.
claims.coverage: All twenty-two arms of the draw phase's dispatcher are ported from its own words; four draw families are ported with per-family oracles running the original routines through the native engine on the shipped binaries, each with a mutation; the draw pass is composed into the session with a headless host; the whole-match verifier reports the mode trajectory before and after.
limitations: The route is not flipped and a match does not complete: the next frame calls the queued-effect-opcode routine, which is unported, followed by several pending phases and mode updates.
The element-panel buckets read no disc catalogue in the headless session, so their counts are zero there; the routine is verified against the original through stubs.
One verifier line about routines absent from the lifted C was corrected, not the generated entry-list artefact itself.
claims.derivation: Ported the duel's draw phase and composed the draw pass, leaving mode one.

claims.statement: The tournament finale is gated on a virtual flag that resolves to the four endgame tamer challenges, and the arena floor's emptiness is the disc's own data - the room is entered rather than walked, and one of our own reachability proofs is stale.
claims.coverage: The gate is decoded from the stage assembly with its branches in order and its predicate-table binding, the floor's record is compared byte for byte between the disc and our extracted data, the arrival event is confirmed by probe, and the finale is reached in our build with the win verifier passing.
limitations: The four challenge producers were cited from an existing document rather than re-decoded.
The stale reachability proof is reported with its fix but not itself corrected in that pass.
One stage's fixture spawn still pins the player at the map origin, which the walk reports and nothing has settled.
claims.derivation: Decoded the finale's gate and compared the arena floor's records against the disc.

claims.statement: The flagged battle routines were never committed as an address list - the pass named them by group - so the flags are settled by mechanism instead, and four mechanisms remain only as browser re-implementations with no pinned address.
claims.coverage: A documented search of the research corpus, the index's full text, the scratch and worktree trees, git history and the transcripts found no roster; the mechanisms the groups name are each classified against the current tree with the audit's per-port consumption column; the four registered routines are shown ported, oracled and consumed.
limitations: Absence of a committed roster is a search result, not proof the pass had none - but the corpora searched are enumerated and the four routines it did register are identified.
The four unpinned mechanisms are named but not yet tied to an original routine.
The research index was stale during the search and was rebuilt by the lead afterwards.
claims.derivation: Searched for the flagged-routine roster, found none, and settled the mechanisms it names against the current tree.

claims.statement: The field's checkerboard transition draws from a packet sequence - thirty cells on an outside-in schedule sliding forty pixels a step - and the field-to-battle transition's own cost, not a leaked hook, is what makes it crawl.
claims.coverage: The routine is forced through the game's own encounter selector and captured across three runs with frame counters, its cell geometry and its live schedule read out, and the frame rate measured at each phase with the hot address deliberately not armed and every hook capped and self-unregistering.
limitations: The reopen stage's direction and rate are not measured (its reverse schedule is a labelled guess), the iris variant did not fire on this route, and the rendered appearance needs a video-memory or primitive dump.
The transition's own cost is measured as a consequence, not explained by which writes dominate it.
Nothing is ported: this is a capture and a decode.
claims.derivation: Captured the checkerboard transition's packet sequence live and measured the frame rate through each phase.

claims.statement: The ordinary route past the opening now passes end to end with no failures, after fixing a stale reachability proof and our own wrong assertion about a stage's spawn.
claims.coverage: The reachability proof performs the gated conversation that a player must have and reaches the arena fight; the walk asserts the disc's own spawn descriptor and the room's hand-off, pinned by a test; the whole walk reports no failures.
limitations: The spawn was read from the committed generated descriptor and corroborated by the running game's own log rather than re-extracted from the raw table.
Two test failures elsewhere are caused by a sibling's in-flight duel files and are not this work's.
A browser walk is the weakest evidence class and cannot establish original behaviour on its own.
claims.derivation: Fixed the stale arena proof and the walk's spawn assertion; the deep walk now passes.

claims.statement: The display-list chain is ported end to end and the shipped geometry is now produced by the port rather than by a hand-written decoder, with the result bit-identical - and the colour path's live capture contained a constant inconsistent with its own outputs, now corrected.
claims.coverage: The mesh arm's packet-field build and cull and the effect mesh's colour path are ports read from the assembly; the extractor runs the ported loop over every shipped file; the regenerated data is compared against a pre-change copy for primitive and vertex equality; the ordinary battle's before and after captures are compared including a same-code noise floor.
limitations: The visibility cull is not wired into the browser render, which has no projection for these meshes, so no visible primitive set changes yet.

The colour path's captured form fixes operand order and the passes but not the light matrix or background colour, so the packed grey is recorded rather than derived; two divergences in the native oracle engine block an end-to-end replay.
No registry rows were added because a sibling held that file.
claims.derivation: Ported the mesh arm and colour path and made the extractor produce shipped geometry through the ported loop.

claims.statement: Our browser's steal attempt rolls a different formula from the original game's: the machine builds a clamped ratio and a technique weight and compares a ten-bit random draw against their product over ten thousand, while the browser rolls a status check on two stats - so a player's steal odds differ from the original's.
claims.coverage: The original routine is read from the overlay assembly with its clamp, its weight shift (which lives in a jump's delay slot), its ten-bit draw and its divisor; the port's oracle spreads across the clamp and boundary cases and fails on a mutation of the divisor; the browser's differing implementation is cited by file and line.
limitations: The effective-stat routine the roll consumes and the record resolver remain host services in the oracle, and the meanings of the ratio's two constants are not re-derived.
The port is not wired into the browser, so what ships is still the divergent formula.
The other three mechanisms are pinned and ported but likewise unconsumed.
claims.derivation: Pinned four browser-only fight mechanisms to their original routines and ported them; the steal roll's formula differs from the browser's.

claims.statement: The duel's between-phase stepper and inspect menu are ports and its queued-effect routine is wired, so a match now runs the effect VM and reaches the inter-phase banner - but it still does not complete, blocking at a board-view widget method the constructor installs.
claims.coverage: Two routine families are ported from their own dispatch tables with their interleaved arms preserved, oracled through the native engine across every dispatch state with mutation controls; a real rotation bug is fixed and the inter-phase tables are materialised from embedded bytes; the whole-match verifier's gap moves one step later and the named-gap count falls.
limitations: A match does not complete: the board view's banner-widget method blocks, and pending phases and modes remain unported, with a hundred and nine effect-layer host edges counted.
