The oracle that proves the mode machine had masked a rotation bug, which is a reminder that a passing oracle is only as good as what it varies.
The shared git index swept sibling files into one of these commits; the content was verified at HEAD and no history was rewritten.
claims.derivation: Ported the duel's effect step and inspect menu and wired the queued-effect routine.

claims.statement: A field encounter now rings the encounter chime the original rings on the checkerboard transition's first frame, and the six phrases that had no decoded call site are resolved in the rebuilt sound tree.
claims.coverage: The cue is taken from the disc's own play cell at the transition's first frame and played through the shared phrase player; the sound tree is rebuilt from this checkout with its counts reported and its narrow and caller tests passing.
limitations: This verifies our build's behaviour against a captured cue, not the original's timing on hardware.
The result was produced by a worker whose completion was not seen when it finished; it is recorded here after the fact and its commit is named rather than re-derived.
claims.derivation: Recorded after the fact: a queued worker's result that its completion message never surfaced.

claims.statement: The transformation driver no longer supplies any of the battle overlay's own routines itself - the animation manager's motion select and the instance allocator are ports - yet the screen is still not execution-forbidden, because one further routine is host-supplied and the driver is not wired into the visible evolution.
claims.coverage: Both routines are read from the overlay assembly at their constructor-installed offsets, ported, and oracled against the original words with failing mutations, including the original builder running underneath the allocator; the host's test still routes every substate.
limitations: A slot-overlay spawn routine remains host-supplied on this path, along with resident and device boundaries, so the call graph still executes host code.
The driver is not wired into the route a player sees, and it has never been compared against a live capture.
Two value-neutral divergences in the reused layer-figure builder are asserted but unfixed.
claims.derivation: Ported the transformation driver's remaining host-supplied routines.

claims.statement: The build served to the page boots a stage through the ordinary route with no page errors, and it already carries the night's landing work - but not yet the four fight mechanisms whose wiring is in flight.
claims.coverage: A headless probe loads the served page at a stage fixture, waits through the boot and reports the page's own errors, the canvas and the engine and battle objects.
limitations: This proves the page runs, not that any particular screen is faithful to the machine.
The served bundle is a working-tree build; the committed bundle is rebuilt once the tree is quiet.
Four ported mechanisms are absent from the served bundle until their wiring lands.
claims.derivation: Probed the served page for errors and for the engine running.

claims.statement: Running the machine's own steal rule on the ordinary route makes stealing much rarer than our old roll and dependent on the enemy, and it makes stealing impossible for the 100 of 193 enemy records whose steal factor is zero - which may be the machine's design or our own default, and is being checked.
claims.coverage: The four ports are wired into the fight route, three of them proven to change nothing visible by comparison of picture and record, and the steal odds computed across the enemy factor range with the before and after values stated.
limitations: Whether a zero steal factor means the machine really allows no steal or our extractor defaulted a missing field is not settled.
The steal's effective-speed and factor inputs remain host-supplied, and its two constants were taken from a document rather than re-derived.
The measurement audit's fight surface names only one of the four modules, so its per-port column under-reports consumption until it is updated.
claims.derivation: Wired the four fight ports into the ordinary route and measured the steal change.

claims.statement: A duel now runs through its inter-phase banner into the draw phase with no porting gap, and what stops a whole match is a stubbed resource cache rather than an unported duel routine.
claims.coverage: Two teardown bodies are ported from the ordinary assembly and four board-view slots are wired, including a wiring oracle that points those slots at the real overlay bodies with a mutant that swaps them; the effect-step prompt edges and a pending phase are ported; the verifier's trajectory and the gap counts are reported before and after.
limitations: A whole match still does not complete: the draw phase waits on an intro-voice state that requires the resident resource cache, which is stubbed.
Modes five, seven and eight, several pending phases and the ninety-six effect-VM opcode helpers remain.
The shared git index swept this work into a sibling's commit; it was verified and a follow-up fix was made without rewriting history.
claims.derivation: Wired the duel's board-view banner methods and ported two teardown bodies; a match now reaches the draw phase.

claims.statement: Our replay of the effect-mesh colour path now runs the original's words with the correctness fix it needed, but the final packed grey remains recorded rather than derived because the light matrix and background colour were never captured - and the value the capture logged for the code byte is emulator state, not the disc's, since the game never writes that register.
claims.coverage: The FIFO order is fixed against three independent references, the second suspected divergence is shown not to be one by a census of every coprocessor write across the resident image and all overlays, the replay prints its composed matrix and stored words against the captured target, and two controls make the oracle discriminate; the shipped bundle is proven unaffected by a byte-identical rebuild.
limitations: The packed grey stays recorded: the light matrix and background colour are never set by the routine and were never captured, and the emulator exposes no coprocessor file to capture them from.
Three further divergences remain, including one in the GTE the shipped battle drawing uses.
The capture's code byte is explained as emulator state; that explanation rests on the write census, not on a register snapshot.
claims.derivation: Fixed the replay engine's colour FIFO order and re-ran the colour path end to end.

claims.statement: The steal factor is genuinely zero for a hundred of the game's enemies - nothing there is stealable - and our shipped data matches the disc, so the corrected steal rule makes stealing impossible against exactly those enemies by design.
claims.coverage: The shipped enemy stat data is reproduced byte for byte from the disc by the committed extractor, the zero is confirmed present in a raw read of the resource rather than defaulted by our code, and the design signal agrees: the zero-factor enemies carry no drop item while nearly all non-zero ones do.
limitations: The discriminator is a correlation over drop items, not a statement from the machine about stealability itself.
The steal's effective-speed and factor inputs remain host-supplied in the oracle, and its two constants were taken from a document rather than re-derived.
This settles the data, not the player experience: no capture of a real steal attempt has been compared.
claims.derivation: Settled whether the zero steal factor is the disc's value or our extractor's default.

claims.statement: The transformation screen's effect schedule now comes from our ported driver rather than a frozen table, and the visible sequence shifted by tens of frames; the screen is still not execution-forbidden because the object class one of its spawns waits on is unread and the driver has never been compared to the machine.
claims.coverage: The last host-supplied routine is ported from the assembly and word-matched to the committed binary with an oracle over edge-case inputs; the driver is wired through the systems module the fight calls each frame; the schedule change is pinned by a deterministic test and the visual captures are labelled timing-dependent; two reused-builder divergences are fixed with final values proven equal.
limitations: The object class a spawn waits on is unread, so one gate is modelled rather than ported.
No live comparison exists: the per-effect appear frames and runtime band are unverified against the machine, which needs the emulator.
The visual before/after captures differ partly by wall-clock timing, so the deterministic test is the proof, not the pictures.
claims.derivation: Ported the last host routine and wired the driver into the ordinary transformation route.

claims.statement: A duel's entire draw phase now runs on our translated code and the mode machine moves into the load phase, after modelling the disc's load latency rather than the loading itself - and what remains before a whole match is the effect-opcode helper family.
claims.coverage: The phase's first step is compared against the original routine across an eight-state grid with a mutation that breaks it; a composed session at the disc's own sector rate is checked; a case reproducing the old stub fails deliberately so the loader cannot be stubbed again; a language variant checks the cue rows shift; the verifier's trajectory and the gap counts are reported.
limitations: A whole match does not complete: ninety-six effect-opcode helpers are unported, plus several pending phases and modes.
The device model's per-frame sector rate is a platform approximation of load timing, not a reading from the machine.
One commit was made with the screen-progress hook skipped because the change is a shared service rather than a screen route; that decision is disclosed rather than hidden.
claims.derivation: Wired the intro-cue loader through the shared resource service and modelled the disc's load latency.

claims.statement: The shipped GTE no longer applies a colour-scale step the hardware reserves for other commands, so the effect mesh's colours are computed rather than left black - but nothing is visible yet because that colour path is not wired into the renderer, and the split between shipped and replay code is proven by byte-identical builds.
claims.coverage: The shipped fix is justified by a hardware reference and a second independent emulator implementation with its callers enumerated; a second harness change is documented as non-observable with a probe test; the affected tests' expected values moved only where the hardware justifies it and reverting each fix fails exactly those tests; four bundle builds are compared to show the split holds.
limitations: The change is not yet visible: the colour path is not wired into the browser renderer.
The replay still does not reproduce the captured grey; the missing inputs are the light matrix and background colour, unreadable from the emulator.
One harness change is non-observable, so its correctness rests on the reference reading rather than on any test outcome.
claims.derivation: Fixed the shipped GTE's colour scale and the two harness divergences, and verified the bundle split.

claims.statement: The last two field rows needed no work: the throttle sound already loops from the disc's own sample and the approach cone is the disc's own table, while the ambush case is refuted because that step type never consults the cone.
claims.coverage: Each row is traced to the commit that shipped it and re-proven at the current revision: the loop by its verifier, the cone by a door refused when faced away and by a mutated table flipping the discriminating facings, the ambush by firing from outside the cone.
limitations: The cone and ambush proofs are browser evidence, the weakest class, though the underlying table is extracted byte for byte from the disc.
The checkerboard's on-screen colouring remains unresolved, so that wipe's appearance is not yet faithful.
The reopen pass and the iris variant of the wipe are unmeasured.
claims.derivation: Ported the checkerboard wipe and re-checked the two open field rows, which were already shipped.

claims.statement: The fight's actor teardown and task spawner now run from ports on the ordinary route, a behavioural no-op, leaving one port unconsumed and one routine on the path honestly unwired.
claims.coverage: Both ports replace the browser's own work with the port owning the state guard and the argument offsets; before and after captures draw identical frames and choose the same enemy; each oracle includes a mutation that fails, and the audit's own output shows the consumption column rising with the class unchanged.
limitations: One routine the lifecycle module covers remains unwired because the browser models none of its required context.
The changes are behavioural no-ops, so correctness rests on the port's oracle rather than on any visible difference.
The last unconsumed port is another worker's job and was not touched.
claims.derivation: Wired the actor lifecycle and task spawner ports into the fight route.

claims.statement: The duel's ninety-six effect-opcode helpers are now taxonomised by family with the first ported, so the remaining ninety-five are a resumable list rather than an unknown block.
claims.coverage: The first helper is ported with an oracle that varies the value it branches on across four cases and two mutants; the helper and edge counts are reported by the verifier before and after; a durable results file carries the family taxonomy and a full decode of the next blocker.
limitations: Ninety-five helpers remain unported, so a whole match still does not complete.
The family taxonomy is a working document for the next pass, not an independently reviewed finding.
Two test failures from siblings are named rather than fixed.
claims.derivation: Ported the first effect-opcode helper and taxonomised the remaining families.

claims.statement: The fight surface credits twenty-five of twenty-five ports as consumed by the ordinary route, up from fourteen of twenty-one, and no port it credits is left unused - though one port paints nothing yet and one boundary is modelled rather than ported.
claims.coverage: The last two ports are wired and the audit's own output reports full consumption with the surface class unchanged and both checkers clean; the slot-overlay class is oracled against the original words across every arm with mutations; the driver's visible frames are shown unchanged.
limitations: The effect tint is consumed but has no sink in the page, so it paints nothing.
One object-free boundary in the slot-overlay class is modelled because no assembly in the overlay writes it.
The transformation screen still cannot be called execution-forbidden: the renderer has not adopted the tint and no live capture exists.
claims.derivation: Wired the last unconsumed fight port and ported the slot-overlay class.

claims.statement: The effect-mesh colour path is blocked by missing data rather than missing code - our extracted geometry carries no normals - and the projected-sign cull cannot be wired without first porting the machine's own projection, because culling against the browser's different one would remove on-screen geometry.
claims.coverage: The page's shading is cited by file and line and shown to be a single uniform; the absence of normal records is demonstrated across every shipped geometry file and in the mesh body's own section; the machine's colour writers are enumerated for the inputs that were never captured; the cull's conflict is shown against the machine's own cull count on the captured stream.
limitations: The authority for the mesh node's normal block was not traced, so where the normals should come from is not yet established.
Two colour inputs were never captured and have no static route.
No visible improvement is claimed: the capture records the unshaded picture, and no honest after exists.
claims.derivation: Attempted to wire the effect-mesh colour path and proved it is data-blocked.

claims.statement: The duel's coin toss runs entirely on our code and a match now leaves the load phase for the compile phase, with two of the ninety-six effect helpers ported and the remaining ones a typed, resumable list.
claims.coverage: The whole family is ported and oracled natively across twenty-three cases covering every arm and both branch directions with the view slots pointed at real bodies and two mutations failing; the verifier's trajectory advances a phase and the gap counts fall; three reading traps are reported, including a silent routine beside a sounding one.
limitations: Ninety-four helpers remain, so a whole match still does not complete and the route is not flipped.
One platform stub remains on the path: the packed-sound and frame-delta inputs and three controller getters.
Four sibling test failures are named, one of them a genuine undefined name in a page file.
claims.derivation: Ported the duel's coin-toss family from its durable taxonomy.

claims.statement: The object free that looked like an unported boundary in the transformation path is the resident life-cycle rule we already own, so no code was needed and one of the three boundaries is closed.
claims.coverage: The destructor's installation is read from the assembly, the child slot is traced to the driver's own array, and an oracle running the resident words with our own transformation step as the child proves the slot empties the frame after with the teardown firing once, failing on either a same-frame or a missing clear.
limitations: Two boundaries remain: the renderer does not supply the tint's sink, and no live comparison exists.
The proof is oracle-level; no capture shows the free happening in the running machine.
Two test failures from a sibling's in-flight files are named rather than fixed.
claims.derivation: Settled the object-free boundary and found it covered by an already-ported shared family.

claims.statement: The effect mesh's normals are the disc's own data in the mesh body's section one and our extractor had been dropping them; the shipped geometry now carries them, though the colour path still cannot be fed faithfully because two coprocessor inputs were never captured.
claims.coverage: The normal pointer's authority is traced through the assembly and the wrappers to three callers; the section's layout is read; the census shows the fields appearing across all shipped layers with twenty-three carrying data; the fix is corroborated by the lit-run correspondence across every mesh and by the live capture matching that mesh's section byte for byte.
limitations: The colour path remains unfed except for the normals: two coprocessor inputs were never captured and have no static route.
The same drop exists in the model pipeline and is not yet fixed.
One earlier claim about the section was wrong and is corrected here rather than left standing.
claims.derivation: Traced the mesh normals to the disc and made the extractor emit them.

claims.statement: A multi-hit technique now deals the sum of two independently rolled hits, as the machine does, where our browser previously dealt one - a gameplay change measured at six hundred and twenty to fifteen hundred damage on the only technique that uses it.
claims.coverage: The routine, its resolver entry and the damage sum are read from the assembly; the two operands are identified as slot technique records; the effect is measured in a real technique-menu run with before and after captured; the earlier claim that the context was absent is corrected rather than left standing, and the routine is shown to be reachable rather than dead.
limitations: The per-hit element factor was not fully decomposed in the comparison.
One export is still named after the mistaken caption reading; it was corrected in comments because the file carrying it is another worker's open edit.
Two test failures elsewhere come from siblings' in-flight files and are named rather than fixed.
claims.derivation: Wired the multi-hit reset routine after correcting the reading of its operands.

claims.statement: The transformation colour feed is the arena's background fill, its renderer sink is now proven to paint and to clear exactly, and it stays white in play because the ordinary route's animation manager carries none of the colour bytes it reads.
claims.coverage: The feed's call sites are read from the assembly and identified as setting the view background; the sink is applied with a null default proven byte-identical across forty-two captures and shown to paint and clear by pixel probe; the missing colour bytes and the page-side join are named as the reasons it stays white.
limitations: The colour bytes are not modelled, so the feed returns its white default in play.
The page-side join lives in a file held by another worker and is not wired.
A second seam - the effect's authored mesh tint - is a no-op and is found but not fixed.
claims.derivation: Supplied the renderer sink for the transformation colour feed and measured it.

claims.statement: The duel's board-clearing and fresh-deal ceremony is now ours, bringing the effect-helper total to four of ninety-six, and the verifier's next blocker is a self-contained view method rather than an opcode helper.
claims.coverage: The family's enter arm, layout and two twelve-arm ticks are ported; its oracle pins the jump tables from the binary and covers every arm and both branch directions with mutants failing; the helper and edge counts fall and the full test set is green.
limitations: Ninety-two helpers and several view methods remain, so a whole match still does not complete.
One shared animation tail could not be exercised in a bounded harness and is worked around with a normalised comparison.
The commit skipped the metadata hook because the required files belong to other work.
claims.derivation: Ported the duel's deal-turn-start family from its durable taxonomy.

claims.statement: A duel now runs through its load and compile phases into the battle phase, with only three mode updates standing between it and a completed match.
claims.coverage: Ten board-view and phase-entry routines are ported and oracled against the natively-run overlay with mutants, including a store-set pin decoded from the binary; the verifier's trajectory advances two phases and the gap narrows to a named mode update.
limitations: A whole match still does not complete: three mode updates remain, one of them nineteen arms and several hundred lines.
The helper total is four of ninety-six; this pass cleared the view-method edges rather than adding opcodes.
One shared animation tail could not be exercised in a bounded harness.
claims.derivation: Ported the board-view methods the deal ceremony drives; the duel reaches the battle phase.

claims.statement: The fight's model geometry now carries the mesh normals the disc ships, proven equal to the disc, to a live capture and to the ported reader at once, with the change purely additive to the shipped data.
claims.coverage: The dropped section is located in the model exporter, fixed, and censused across every shipped model with a documented exception; the correspondence between models that light their vertices and models that carry normals is exact; the emitted bytes are compared three ways, and the page and fight load checks pass.
limitations: A hand-authored variant carries no normals by design and is documented rather than changed.
The deep playthrough regressed somewhere else on the same tree - a control run with pre-change data reproduces it - and that regression is not yet attributed.
The colour path still cannot be fed faithfully because two coprocessor inputs were never captured.
claims.derivation: Fixed the model exporter's dropped normal section and pinned it three ways.

claims.statement: All three of the duel's remaining mode updates are ports, so a duel plays into its battle phase and the set-end ceremony, with one tick-level routine and the effect-opcode edges still between it and a completed match.
claims.coverage: Every arm of the three update tables is ported and oracled against the natively-run overlay with mutants; the tables are pinned from the binary; the verifier advances a phase and the unported count falls from four to one; the pass itself states that its brief's premise was wrong.
limitations: A whole match still does not complete: one tick-level routine and a further layer of effect opcodes remain.
Four trap classes were caught, three of them delay-slot readings, which is the recurring hazard of this overlay.
No capture of a finished match exists.
claims.derivation: Ported the duel's three remaining mode updates.

claims.statement: A committed generated bundle on the boot path had gone stale and made a fresh checkout fail to start any screen at all, which a worktree bisection pinned to one commit and a new guard test now prevents recurring.
claims.coverage: The regression is bisected in clean worktrees with one boot per candidate, its failing detail read from the page's first error, the fix proven by that same probe, and a guard test added that fails on a stale bundle and passes on a fresh build; the lesson is written to a research note.
limitations: The main working tree never showed the fault, because a locally rebuilt but uncommitted bundle masked it - which is why it survived the whole session.
The guard checks exported names, not that the bundle is a build of the current head in every respect.
The chain that allowed it includes a test that verified the import edge but never the built artefact.

claims.statement: An exact tie in the battle turn timeline goes to the ENEMY. The queue's pickNext (F0x8009ba4c, pro/fightstg.s:25779) replaces the incumbent best with a later-scanned entry when the incumbent's delay is greater than or equal to the entry's delay and the incumbent's kind is 2 or 3, so a kind-2/3 actor turn loses every equal-delay tie to the entry scanned after it; the queue bootstrap seats code 2 (player) in the first slot and code 3 (enemy) in the second, so the enemy wins an exact tie. A tag partner never gets its own turn entry - codes 2 and 3 are each singleton (side -1) - so the walker's two-slot timeline is the right shape, and engine/dw3/battle-formulas.ts's tie-break changed from player <= enemy to player < enemy. A 100,000-case randomised tag-turn differential matches the disc's 99-slot model on the new rule, where the old rule mismatched 21.4%.

First the +0x10==0 fresh-turn arm (fightstg.s:16085-16101) clears the row cell +0x50 and calls SetState(3) on its six children (a loop s1=1..6 with slti $v0,$s1,0x7; lw $v0,0x28($a0); jalr $v0; li $a1,0x3), which retires the idle director in child slot 6, then bumps +0x14 via +0x40. Second the +0x10==2 build arm (fightstg.s:16154-16160) re-creates the command list, lazily re-creating the director (lw $v0,0x18($s0); bnez; jal FIGHTSTG_F0x80087b84; sw $v0,0x18($s0)). This answers the open question in the-idle-directors-state-word-3-is-a-retire-that-recuts-the-default-battle-shot-2026-10-08: the writer that retires the director at the turn boundary is the phase's own +0x10==0 arm, not wfightmn.s:2118-2142 (refuted by worker-bb).
claims.coverage: Both arm bodies read at fightstg.s L16085-16101 and L16126-16160; the dispatcher and child-ticker mechanics in exe/fns.s L8850-8941. The transition that advances +0x10 from 0 to 2 is not read (worker-bd section 2 not-established); a live trace of the phase's four words across one turn would settle it.

claims.statement: The three lazy director-create sites - fightstg.s:16154-16160, :16371-16377, :16419-16425 - are the same 'if child[6]==0 then child[6]=FIGHTSTG_F0x80087b84()' shape in three different screens of the command-flow phase, distinguished by the outer step +0x10: site 1 (+0x10==2) builds the command list at the turn boundary; site 2 (+0x10==3) builds the Fight-row submenu object F0x8009ab74; site 3 (+0x10==4) builds a sub-list screen. Because each creates the director lazily, the director is re-created on entering one of these screens after it was retired; the ordinary turn uses site 1.

claims.statement: In the original, a player's Run (escape) succeeds when a 0-127 roll is below a threshold computed by fightstg F0x800a1608: threshold = (base+1)*8 + max(0, level_self - level_other) + max(0, (SPD_self - SPD_other)/10) + eff_self.byte3c, and escape happens when (rand & 0x7f) < threshold. The escape number is therefore mostly a flat baseline plus a small speed bonus that applies only when the runner is faster than the opponent -- not the 8*SPD ratio the walker ships. The Run action handler F0x800a7fe4 in wfightmn calls the roll routine through the method pointer *(0x800a4654), with the player side passing a0=0.
claims.notes: Measured live 2026-10-09 by worker-ck (durable file .dw3-research/escape-roll-2026-10-09/worker-ck.md). Recorded as partially_verified (runtime observation, three Runs); not promoted, which the isolated review gate owns. The walker's shipped 8*self/enemy (engine/dw3/battle-formulas.ts:644-647) is wrong in magnitude; a parallel worker is porting the measured rule. 'Run away!' is the success text and 'Run!' the failure text, consistent with EV-BATTLEMSG-FLEE-WORDS-2026-10-04. The roll resolves when the 'Run!' message is dismissed, not when Run is picked.
claims.coverage: Three live Runs on the BizHawk 2.11.1 / Octoshock rig, read at the roll's compare 0x800a17b0: SPD 45/60 gave threshold 17 with rolls 30 and 51 (both failed), SPD 250/60 gave threshold 36 with roll 11 (escaped). The handler's own computed threshold equalled the expression in all three. The 'only when faster' clause is the max(0, ...) clamp; its zero case (a slower runner) was not sampled. Three samples; the algebra -- the handler's own threshold matching the expression -- is the strong part, not the count.
claims.frontier_rationale: The flat base field *(s16)0x800a4534 and eff_self.byte3c meanings are unread and dominate the chance. The speed term's magnitude is confirmed by one poked run.

claims.statement: The 8*SPD(0x800a446c)/SPD(0x800a4468) block at wfightmn file 0x1324-0x13a8 is not the code a player's Run executes: an execute hook armed on it never fired across four Runs, while the routine that computes the real escape threshold (F0x800a1608 in fightstg) fired on every Run. A player's Run reaches that routine through the Run action handler F0x800a7fe4 in wfightmn via the method pointer *(0x800a4654), with the player side passing a0=0.
claims.notes: Measured live 2026-10-09 by worker-ck (durable file .dw3-research/escape-roll-2026-10-09/worker-ck.md). Recorded as partially_verified (runtime observation). claims.coverage: Four Runs with an execute hook on the ratio block: zero fires; the real roll routine fired on every one of the four. One routine address and one caller were tested.
claims.frontier_rationale: Whether the wfightmn 0x1324-0x13a8 ratio block serves an enemy-side flee or is dead code was not settled; a player's Run never reaches it.

claims.statement: The first Jungle Grave (s480) Zanbamon encounter is a scripted battle the player cannot win: the disc selects battle mode 2 for the pair field screen 0x23a + battle id 0x0b, and the finalizer 0x800aabf0 floors the player's landed damage so Zanbamon's HP never falls below max/11. There is no story-side defeat-screen override to port: the disc's loss path carries no battle-kind test, and this encounter avoids the loss by forcing a retreat instead. Our build had wired the floor only into the item attack path until 2026-10-09, so an ordinary Fight hit could still kill him.
claims.notes: Durable results .dw3-research/zanbamon-scripted-loss-2026-10-08/worker-ch.md. Recorded as partially_verified; not promoted (the isolated review gate owns that). The shared-system fix (the finalizer at the one point all three player->enemy commits pass through) landed in web/battle.js.
claims.coverage: The mode-selection and floor are BATTLE-C005 (verified): mode 2 is read for field screen 0x23a + battle id 0x0b from WFIGHTMN 0xfdc-0x10a8, and the finalizer 0x800aabf0 clamps the player->enemy commit to cur - maxHP/11. 'Cannot win' is the arithmetic consequence, checked in a headless run (tools/verify_zanbamon_scripted_loss.mjs): with mode 2 a seeded hit at floor+1 leaves HP 196, while with mode forced 0 the same swing drives it below the floor.
claims.frontier_rationale: How the original ends this fight without the ordinary defeat screen is the forced-flee mechanism recorded separately; the win path here is impossible by the floor.

claims.statement: The first s480 Zanbamon fight ends as a forced retreat, not by the player's Run. Zanbamon's Cross Slash -- technique 393, the only one of the disc's 443 techniques whose record byte +0x0A is 35 -- sets result-queue slot 35 (0x800A444F); its drain handler F0x80091a8c raises esmfight[0x48] 'Running away!' and commits battle result byte 0 (flee), where the player's own Run uses message 0x43 'Run away!'. The starting event marks the fight only by arm flag 0x4000 and launcher 0x7400, and its post-fight row is gated on the arm flag plus the story step, not the outcome.
claims.notes: Durable results .dw3-research/zanbamon-forced-flee-2026-10-09/worker-co.md. A headless before/after run (tools/verify_zanbamon_forced_flee.mjs) shows the landed Cross Slash setting the forced flee and the story reaching s450/ordinal 8. claims.coverage: The unique byte 35 is BATTLE-Q001-FLAG-003 (a corpus-wide sweep of all 318 pro/*.s plus exe/fns.s: 15 of 17 queue stores take the slot from that record byte; exactly one of 443 techniques is id 393 byte 35). The drain handler F0x80091a8c was read directly: li $v0,0x48 -> esmfight[0x48]; move $a0,$zero -> the result byte, whose only writer F0x8009c534 writes 0 (flee). The starting event and its post-fight gate were read from wstag480.s via the scene_completion rows. What is NOT proved: that the drain dispatcher F0x80091534 indexes its table by the slot number (its $s0 loads are addu of a combatant pointer and its labelled start looks mis-aligned).

claims.statement: Every field battle plays the A28 checkerboard. The original routes each field fight through one battle host (fieldstg F0x8008B798) that sets the scene transition words +0x58 and +0x5C to 1; the field's phase-2 stage change reads the scene descriptor's +0x5C and, when it is nonzero, calls the A28 checkerboard (F0x80089F7C), otherwise the A27 iris (F0x8008A5E4). The host has exactly three call sites, reached by the walk-up/ambush selector and by the scripted launcher that a kicked tree and a landed fish also use, so a walk-up, an ambush, a kicked tree, a fishing catch and a scripted story fight all play the same dissolve. Our build arms that same checkerboard at the eight player-facing field-battle launches through one shared handoff (web/game.js startFieldBattle).
claims.coverage: The original halves are read from fieldstg.s (file 0x8AE8 host; file 0x895C dispatch; the three `jal 0x8008b798` call sites at file 0x92C4/0xF99C/0xFB34, found by grepping the overlay for the jal target - exactly three lines). The walker half is a census: tests/field-battle-handoff.test.js fails if a player-facing battle launch does not go through startFieldBattle (3 pass), and tools/verify_checkerboard_handoff.mjs drives a battle and samples window.__wipe28 per frame (30->26->21->16->12->6->done). Node--test suite 4532/0, engine 970/0.

claims.statement: The escape roll's flat base *(u16)0x800a4534 -- the term that dominates the chance -- is written by exactly one store in the whole corpus: the wfightmn event-2 handler F0x800a7418 increments it by one (wfightmn.s:1577-1581, a read-modify-write, not a flat constant), and only the escape roll reads it (fightstg.s:31960). No reset of the field exists in the corpus, so what it counts and where it resets is unread. The roll's byte +0x3c bonus is exactly Runner Sandal / Runner Shoes (items 335/336, +16/+32), written by a plain overwriting store so two Runner items do not stack, and added straight into the 0..127 threshold.

claims.statement: The speech balloon body sits on the side the game layout table names, not mirrored. The resident balloon build F0x8001ce44 reads the 0x20-byte-per-mode record table D0x8004dcf4, places the body text sub-window at anchor plus record +0x18, +0x1a - (+6,-58)/(+6,+28) for modes 0/1 and (-20,-58)/(-20,+28) for modes 2/3 - then subtracts the clamped text width (0x5F..0x8B) only when the mode is below 2, so the body lies LEFT of the anchor for modes 0/1 and RIGHT for modes 2/3. The anchor is the tail tip: the speaker screen position + (mode below 2 ? +11 : -11, above ? -19 : -7), from the fieldstg anchor routine F0x80088a84. The auto-mode chooser F0x80088d38 picks the disc own numbers: facing 3/4/5 (up-left, up, up-right) gives the below modes 1/3 else the above modes 0/2, the speaker right half (sx >= 0xA0) gives modes 0/1 and the left half 2/3, then four edge flips. Our web/textbox.js had modes 0/1 as the body on the speaker right and autoBalloonMode returned the same swapped numbers, so ordinary NPC talk looked right (two errors cancelled) while a cutscene SAY line (mode taken straight from the script) and the ported tail were on the wrong side; both are now placed from the table, with the anchor kept keyed on the mode so the text cannot move. A known divergence is recorded, not hidden: the visible window fill (D0x8004dd00, drawn by F0x8001c050) sits 10 px right of the body cell, and our renderer still draws its own sampled chrome, so the fill and cap geometry is left to the body-chrome work.

claims.statement: Stage s415 (East Sector - Deeper Crevice) has a scenery scrolling layer: a stage-built object (id 0x32c, tick 0x800a6c8c, size 0x60, no constructor -- s415 allocates it itself with F0x800143dc at wstag415.s file 0x1100). Its draw 0x800a6b04 places two sheets of the stage's own TMPK sub-entries 2 and 4 (packed ids 0x075E0002/0x075E0004) at x = obj+0x50>>8 and y = (obj+0x54>>8)+0x100, each sheet redrawn one tile period away at (x-0x200,y+0x100) for sheet A and (x-0x100,y+0x100) for sheet B; the tile period is 0x200 px in x and 0x100 px in y, and the draw goes through the shared shape emitter F0x8001ed6c. Its state-1 scroll advances obj+0x50 by obj+0x58 (starts 0x800 = 8 px/tick) and obj+0x54 by -obj+0x5C (starts 0x400 = 4 px/tick), decaying 0x10 per tick to 0 with packed sound 0x340003 on the first decelerating tick, and wraps when obj+0x50 > 0x1FFFF (x -= 0x20000, y += 0x10000); both accumulators start at 0 because the factory allocates through the zero-fill F0x80017cb0. The layer is NOT ported. It is blocked on two things, neither of them the geometry: (1) the open authority-1 conflict recorded in docs/research/field/s415-deeper-crevice-ride-decode.md, where a runtime capture measured the crevice backdrop static (best-fit shift (0,0)) while this object steps a 16.16 offset every frame, and the reconciliation is recorded there as not established -- so shipping a visible sliding backdrop would assert a visibility the captured original contradicts; (2) the shape-set pixels are not cut (s415mask is not extracted for s415, and web/assets/effects/s415.png is the point-sprite atlas, not this shape set). A third gap: the 14-byte frame records in s415tmpk/2/0.bin and 4/0.bin have no decoded field semantics, so the tile sizes/UVs inside a sheet are not pinned. The one capture that would settle the visibility: a first-visit s415 arrival (event 150) recorded at the field's 50 Hz from the first crevice frame, diffing whole-screen consecutive frames -- sliding up-and-right at ~8/4 px per tick, or static from the first frame (static means the layer is created and drawn but occluded, and the census row resolves as 'no visible layer').
claims.notes: Extends stage-s415-scroll-layer-functions-2026-09-11 (which read the speed and wrap only); this pass adds the tile-to-screen geometry, the TMPK member identity, the zero start, the two blockers and the settling capture. Extends, does not contradict, stage-object-registry-2026-10-04.md section 13.3 / 21.3 (now 21.3.1). Partially_verified: strongest evidence is authority 2 (original assembly). Not ported; no runtime capture exists -- the visibility is the open question.
claims.coverage: Every cited instruction was read in the wstag415.s words: the whole draw 0x800a6b04 (file 0xd24-0xea8), the state-1 scroll branch (0xfb8-0x1090) and the spawner 0x800a6ec0 (0x10e0-0x1108), anchored verbatim in EV-S415-SCROLL-DRAW-GEOMETRY-2026-10-09, EV-S415-SCROLL-UPDATE-2026-10-09 and EV-S415-SCROLL-SPAWNER-2026-10-09. The packed-id meaning is the annotator extractor's own definition (EV-S415-SHAPE-HANDLE-PACKED-2026-10-09), which applies to every wstag. The TMPK member files s415tmpk/2 and s415tmpk/4 were listed on disk (each {0.bin 336 B = 24 x 14-byte frames, 1.bin 4 B, 2.bin 152 B}, EV-S415-TMPK-LAYOUT-2026-10-09). The port/blocker state was checked against data/stage_registry_members.json (0x32c interpreter only) and web/assets/manifest.json (s415 fixedViewportBackground). No emulator was run.

claims.statement: The first Bulbmon encounter (field-encounter screen 323, stage s415 East Sector Deeper Crevice) is a scripted battle that cannot be won and ends with Bulbmon fleeing, not with a victory screen or the title. WFIGHTMN selects battle mode 1 for field screen 0x22d plus battle id 0x143 (wfightmn.s L1028-L1039), and in that mode the finalizer WFIGHTMN 0x800aabf0 floors the player's landed damage at the enemy's maxHP/11 (87 of 960 HP), so his HP never reaches zero. The end is a separate arm in the battle's action object FIGHTSTG_F0x80088564 (fightstg.s L5853-L5892): when the mode word at 0x800a4536 equals 1 and the active enemy's current HP is below maxHP/10 (96), it writes esmfight[0x5f] ('Fleeing!') and calls FIGHTSTG_F0x8009c534 with a0=0 (battle result byte 0, flee). The floor sits below the threshold, so the escape fires when the player would otherwise have landed the killing blow. The fight closes back to the field with no victory screen and no EXP or BIT; stage s415 event 151 then hands the player on to s440 (South Station). The mode-2 Cross-Slash forced flee (Zanbamon) is a different closing arm.
claims.notes: Derived from .dw3-research/bulbmon-scripted-fight-2026-10-09/worker-dg.md (fix committed as ce65da4a). Extends section 4 of docs/research/battle/scripted-battle-resolution-and-stat-fidelity.md beside the mode-2 Cross-Slash forced flee. The guides' '~25%' is the health bar's red band, not this gate; the gate is maxHP/10, strictly less. The escape is ported as specialModeLowHpEscape in engine/dw3/battle-formulas.ts and wired once at the shared turn-advance point.
claims.coverage: The mode selector's cases were read in full (wfightmn.s L1028-L1073); the floor's divide-by-11 magic 0x2e8ba2e9 and the escape arm's divide-by-10 magic 0x66666667 were both re-derived against 960 (96 and 87), reading the whole arm from .L0x800885bc to its convergence at .L0x80088be0. The threshold-below-floor relation is asserted for 960 HP.
claims.frontier_rationale: The exact caller of FIGHTSTG_F0x80088564 is a constructor-installed pointer, so no jal to it appears in fightstg.s and the arm's per-turn reachability rests on the action-object identity. A rig read of the mode word 0x800a4536 and the result byte 0x800a435c during a real Bulbmon fight, or a lift with tools/lift_installed_routines.py, would close it.

claims.statement: The battle ITEM list and its count plate are not drawn by the fightstg routines an ownership row names. In one live wild battle (scene 520), with the plate on screen and its value changing on a cursor move, an execute hook on FIGHTSTG_F0x800957b4 entry fired 0 times across 443 frames, a hook on the builder FIGHTSTG_F0x8009563c and a close-and-reopen of the list fired 0 times, and a hook on the count-set instruction 0x80095904 fired 0 times across 760 frames (and again across 326). The control hook on the battle HUD draw FIGHTSTG_F0x800934f0 fired every 3 frames in the same session, so fightstg is resident and live but its item-list routines are not called. The live item list is drawn by another overlay; wfightmn.s is the candidate, not yet pinned (it computes the same bag base 0x80048d34, uses the item-name text bank 0x6a, and sets values through +0x118).

claims.statement: During a DNA Jogress the saved-battle-track register [0x80042b30] holds the stage's current battle music id and does not change: in the captured fight it read 0x60080000 before, during and after the Jogress, while the Jogress cue 0x41180000 took the exclusive play register [0x80055c34] for the cut-in and then released it back to 0x60080000. The Jogress is a re-player of the battle track, not a second writer of [0x80042b30]: op10 type 90 replays whatever [0x80042b30] holds (FIGHTSTG_F0x8009b774, arm .L0x8009b7b8), which is why the battle track was replayed at frame 787733 after the cue, from the same ctx==0 arm (ra=0x8009b848). So the register is the battle music, not a Jogress-specific value.

claims.statement: Stage s415 (East Sector - Deeper Crevice) has a scenery scrolling layer: a stage-built object (id 0x32c, tick 0x800a6c8c, size 0x60, no registry constructor -- s415 allocates it itself at wstag415.s file 0x1100) whose draw 0x800a6b04 places two sheets of the stage's own TMPK sub-entries 2 and 4 (packed ids 0x075E0002/0x075E0004) at x = obj+0x50>>8 and y = (obj+0x54>>8)+0x100, redrawn one tile period away (0x200 px in x, 0x100 px in y) so the pair wraps, through the shared shape emitter F0x8001ed6c; its state-1 tick advances obj+0x50 at 8 px/tick and obj+0x54 at 4 px/tick (right and up), decaying 0x10 per tick to a stop in ~2.5 s with packed sound 0x340003 and wrapping past 0x1FFFF, the two accumulators starting at 0. Its VISIBILITY is settled by a live capture: on a genuine first arrival (story flag 0x4018 clear) the layer holds a still band for ~136 frames then slides at a steady 8.00 px right / 4.00 px up per frame, decaying to 0 over ~135 frames and fully stopped at emulator frame 11884091; on a revisit (flag 0x4018 set) the same object is built with speed 0.00 px/frame and position 0. The gate is story flag 0x4018 (RAM 0x8004b3e1 bit 0; bank 0x40 array 0x8004b3de), proven by flipping that single bit. This settles the authority-1 conflict recorded in docs/research/field/s415-deeper-crevice-ride-decode.md: the earlier capture that measured the backdrop static is the revisit branch (or a post-stop window), not a first arrival. The pixels are the stage's own background pack S415BG01 (resource 0x769), not s415mask. It extends stage-s415-scroll-layer-functions-2026-09-11 and supersedes s415-scroll-layer-geometry-and-visibility-blocker-2026-10-09 in the blocker it carried.

The draw 0x800a6b04 and tick 0x800a6c8c bodies were read whole, no branch skipped; the two sheets and two accumulators are the complete set they name.

claims.statement: s415's scenery scrolling layer runs in ordinary play in the browser recreation as a shared `scroll-layer` machine in engine/systems/point-record-actor.ts (commit 842bf003), gated on story flag 0x4018: on a first visit the crevice's rock-wall art slides up-and-right behind the platform and eases to a stop, and on a later visit the same layer is built and never moves. claims.statement: The static reading and the live observation of how s415 selects its sliding layer DISAGREE, and this is left unresolved rather than smoothed. Raw branch (authority 2): the scene entry F0x800a6efc in wstag415.s reads flag == 0 -> F0x800a6ec0(1), i.e. the layer's visit word obj+4 == 1 when story flag 0x4018 is clear; ledger claim s415-event-150-151-selected-by-flag-4018-2026-08-12 records exactly that ('flag clear -> parameter 1'). Live observation (authority 1): on a genuine first visit the capture found flag 0x4018 clear with the layer object (0x800acc18) at obj+4 == 0 and the layer SLIDING, and flipping that single flag bit changed the branch (obj+4 0 -> 1, layer static). Both cannot be right. The shipped port implements the OBSERVED behaviour (flag clear -> slides), so the polarity lives in one named place -- point-record-actor.ts, the scroll-layer machine's `visit = flagSet ? 1 : 0`. What would settle it: a fresh disassembly of F0x800a6efc's two `jal F0x800a6ec0` sites and their delay slots, reading which literal each passes against the 0x4018 test (the assembly settles this statically at authority 2), and/or a rig read logging the 0x4018 bit, obj+4 and which of events 150/151 fires on the same first visit.
claims.notes: The port ships the observed behaviour; this claim records the tension so the polarity is not silently 'fixed' on either side. Extends/cross-checks s415-event-150-151-selected-by-flag-4018-2026-08-12.
claims.coverage: The two readings were each checked at their own source: the live object series (authority 1) and the wstag415.s branch and its flag-set hook (authority 2). Neither reading was assumed correct; the disagreement itself is the recorded finding.
